issues.legal_issue: A regrant of family property to one member of a family benefits the family as a whole.
material_facts: The land had been attached to a hereditary village office and was regranted to one family member after an application in which the head of the family had consented to the regrant.
The dispute concerned whether the benefit of that regrant belonged only to the recipient or also to the family.
issues.conclusion: The benefit of a regrant to any member of the family enures to the whole family.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principles stated in Nagesh Bisto Desai v. Khando Tirmal Desai, Kalgonda Babgonda Patil v. Balgonda Kalgonda Patil, and New Kenilworth Hotels (P) Ltd. v. Ashoka Industries Ltd.: a grant to one family member benefits the family as a whole.

predicates.family_property_regrant_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a regrant of property connected with a family belongs only to its recipient or benefits the family.
predicates.regrant_made_to_family_member: The property was regranted to a person who was a member of the family.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns a regrant of family property made to one family member, the regrant benefit belongs to the family as a whole.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant who, by conduct or silence, leads another to rely to that person's detriment on an apparent acceptance of a property transaction may be estopped from later challenging it.
material_facts: The claimant had consented to the regrant of the land to a family member who later transferred it to purchasers.
The claimant lived jointly with the transferring family member and was found to have known of related proceedings concerning the land.
The claimant did not challenge the transfer for about ten years, while the purchasers asserted their rights and participated in successive proceedings concerning the property.
The claimant sought a declaration of absolute ownership, although the property had been described as family property.
issues.conclusion: The claimant was estopped from challenging the alienation, and the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 115 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 bars a person from denying a fact where that person's declaration, act, or omission caused or permitted another to believe it to be true and act on that belief. Estoppel requires conduct amounting to a representation, action on its faith, and resulting detriment; acquiescence may be inferred from conduct, and silence is relevant where there is a duty to speak. The Court relied on Sunderabai v. Devaji Shankara Deshpande, S. Shanmugam Pillai v. K. Shanmugam Pillai, Provash Chandra Dalui v. Biswanath Banerjee, and Indira Bai v. Nand Kishore, among other authorities.

rule.if: property_claim_challenging_alienation and claimant_conduct_indicated_assent and claimant_knew_of_transaction_or_proceedings and claimant_failed_to_object and purchaser_relied_to_detriment

predicates.property_claim_challenging_alienation: The proceeding is a property claim in which a claimant seeks to challenge an alienation.
predicates.claimant_conduct_indicated_assent: The claimant's words, acts, or silence reasonably conveyed acceptance of the transaction to the person who later acquired an interest.
predicates.claimant_knew_of_transaction_or_proceedi: The claimant knew of the transaction or of proceedings concerning the property.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_object: The claimant did not object to the transaction despite having an opportunity to do so.
predicates.purchaser_relied_to_detriment: The purchaser acted on the apparent acceptance and would suffer detriment if the claimant were permitted to challenge the transaction.

issues.definition: A claimant in a property challenge is estopped when the claimant's apparent assent, knowledge, and failure to object lead a purchaser to rely to that purchaser's detriment.
